title: Somnia Collection - IDE Fundamentals Final Project
text:
This project was done in collaboration with OpenAI. We were asked by the design team to create an application of AI that goes beyond language models.
My team and I designed a sleep agent called Somnia. This device collects collection is designed to enhance the sleep experience by incorporating features such as a built in white noise machine, wireless charging, and a smart alarm clock that wakes you up with light instead of sound. The sleep agent also incorporates sounds from a user’s environment to create a personalized sleep experience. For example, if the sleep agent detects that there is a lot of noise in the user’s environment, it can play white noise to help drown out the noise and create a more peaceful sleep environment.


Different levels of prototyping were used throughout the design process, including low fidelity prototyping to quickly test out different ideas and concepts, as well as high fidelity prototyping to create a more polished and realistic representation of the final product. The low fidelity prototypes were created using materials such as cardboard, foam, and paper, while the high fidelity prototypes were created using 3D modeling software and 3D printing.

title: Transdisciplinary Practices Module Final Project: Microplastic Detector
text:
Transdisciplinary Practices is a module in the IDE program that focuses on futures design. In groups of four, we were given photographs of objects that one person uses throughout a day. We decided what their life in London would look like in 2035 and then designed an object that they will use every day.
The design process began with analyzing the objects that our persona used in their current daily life. We then identified five main areas that will change in the future: Microplastics, Homegrown, Cooking Tools, Ingredients, and Reading Materials. We then brainstormed how these areas might change in the future and how they might interact with each other.



Objects with Design Thinking Porcess


We then decided to design a microplastic detector that a private chef could use in the future to ensure the food they are preparing is free of microplastics. We explored futures thinking for a scenario where microplastics have led to a global fertility crisis. This was followed by low fidelity prototyping.



Low Fidelity Prototyping





Low Fidelity Prototyping


Our final prototype was a handheld device that uses spectroscopy to detect microplastics in food. It has a small screen that displays the results and a button to start the analysis. This product has different scanning heads to account for differen types of food.



Final Render





Render in Use





Different Head Attachments

title: LAIR Machine Learning Research Intern
text:
While working at the Laboratory for Autonomous and Intelligent Robotics (LAIR), I conducted research on the biomechanics of skateboarding, utilizing 3D calibration techniques to track and analyze movement in DeepLabCut.
First, my lab partner and I conducted secondary research on biomechanics and experimented position tracking in DeepLabCut.



Preliminary Results from Pen Tracking


We established an end-to-end workflow for data acquisition and analysis, which involved recording skateboarders and applying 3D calibration to extract meaningful insights from the captured footage.



Three Go Pro Camera Set Up for Calibration and Position Tracking


My work involved performing inverse dynamics to measure the kinematic forces exerted on joints, providing valuable insights into the physical demands of skateboarding.
This research not only deepened my understanding of biomechanics but also enhanced my ability to apply advanced analytical tools to real-world applications in robotics and human movement studies.



Results Compared to Camera


We also developed a lesson plan to be used by the professor in his biomechancs course, which included a detailed walkthrough of the data acquisition and analysis process, as well as the interpretation of results. This lesson plan aimed to educate students on the practical applications of machine learning in biomechanics and robotics.

title: E80: Experimental Engineering Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV)
text: This project challenged us to design and build an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) capable of collecting data from various sensors while submerged. We configured a pressure sensor, a temperature sensor, and a microphone to gather environmental data during deployment. The project was a collaborative effort with a team of three other engineering students, and we successfully deployed the AUV in Dana Point, CA.

title: E80: Experimental Engineering Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV)
text: This project challenged us to design and build an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) capable of collecting data from various sensors while submerged. We configured a pressure sensor, a temperature sensor, and a microphone to gather environmental data during deployment. The project was a collaborative effort with a team of three other engineering students, and we successfully deployed the AUV in Dana Point, CA.

title: E80: Experimental Engineering Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV)
text:
About the Project
Using PVC pipes, we designed a robot that could withstand the pressure of being submerged in water and protect the internal electronics. We also designed a waterproofing system to prevent water from damaging the sensors and electronics. The AUV was equipped with a pressure sensor to measure depth, a temperature sensor to monitor water temperature, and a microphone to capture underwater sounds.
The drawings are shown below.



Top View Drawing





Isometric View Drawing


As well as the customized microphone circuit we designed using an op-amp to amplify the signal from the microphone and a bandpass filter to isolate the frequencies of interest. 
This was our robot after first deployment. Unfortunately, the waterproofing system failed and water got into the robot, damaging the sensors and electronics. We learned a lot from this experience and were able to improve our design for future deployments. 
At Dana Point, we deployed the AUV and collected data from the sensors. We were able to successfully gather data on depth, temperature, and underwater sounds. The findings are in the report below.

title: Sit Still
text:
Sit Still is a phrase many Black girls hear while getting their hair braided, pressed, or styled. It is a reminder of both generational love and hardship. Hair has long been politicized: during the transatlantic slave trade, enslaved Africans were forced to shave their heads, erasing cultural identity. Bias against natural Black hair persists today, shaped by centuries of oppression.
This chair reflects that history. Throne-like, yet reminiscent of prison bars, it references both resilience and the ongoing inequities embedded in systems like mass incarceration, permitted under the 13th Amendment in the United States today.
Using found materials, I experimented with human hair trimmings collected from local salons, felting it into a quilted upholstery textile. Like enslaved artisans who crafted tools and furniture from scraps, I transformed what was overlooked into something structural and dignified. The salon, central to both Black and Latinx communities and to my own heritage, grounds this work. By reclaiming hair waste and scrap metal, I center regeneration, identity, and care in my design practice.

title: Bladed Disk Simulation - E171 Final Project
text: Modeled a bladed disk system as a chain of coupled spring–mass oscillators to study how structural variations affect vibration behavior in mechanical systems. Each oscillator represents a turbine blade, with stiffness representing blade flexibility and coupling springs representing interactions between neighboring blades.

title: Bladed Disk Simulation - E171 Final Project
text: Modeled a bladed disk system as a chain of coupled spring–mass oscillators to study how structural variations affect vibration behavior in mechanical systems. Each oscillator represents a turbine blade, with stiffness representing blade flexibility and coupling springs representing interactions between neighboring blades.

title: Bladed Disk Simulation - E171 Final Project
text:
Technical Details

Approach We derived equations of motion for a 2DOF spring–mass system and extended the model to an N-degree-of-freedom system. We then formulated the system as a matrix eigenvalue problem, solved for natural frequencies and mode shapes in MATLAB for a 50-DOF system and analyzed the effect of varying the coupling ratio between blades.
Perfectly Periodic System We assumed that the blades were perfectly periodic, meaning that all blades had the same mass and stiffness. This allowed us to simplify the equations of motion and solve for the natural frequencies and mode shapes of the system.
